disclaimer: threesock is an engineering readiness aid, not an audit. SOC 2 is attested by a licensed CPA firm against your organization's system description and commitments. A codebase can only demonstrate part of the criteria; the rest (board oversight, HR, vendor contracts, physical security) must be evidenced outside the repo. Use this report to find gaps early, not to claim compliance.

topFixes.title: Hard-coded Stripe live key
topFixes.recommendation: Revoke and rotate the credential first, then remove it from the code and load it from a secrets manager or environment variable. Rewriting git history does not un-leak a pushed secret.

topFixes.title: Environment file committed: .env
topFixes.recommendation: Rotate any credentials the file contains, remove it from git with `git rm --cached`, add `.env*` to .gitignore, and commit a .env.example with empty values instead.

topFixes.title: JWTs accepted with the "none" algorithm
topFixes.recommendation: Always verify tokens with an explicit algorithm allow-list, and check exp, aud and iss. Use decode only for logging-free inspection of already-verified tokens.

topFixes.title: Untrusted PR code checked out in a privileged workflow (.github/workflows/ci.yml)
topFixes.recommendation: Use the pull_request trigger for anything that builds or tests PR code. Keep pull_request_target for labelling or commenting, without checking out the head.

topFixes.title: Publicly accessible database: aws_db_instance.main
topFixes.recommendation: Turn off public accessibility, place the database in private subnets, and reach it through the application, a bastion or a private endpoint.

findings.title: Untrusted PR code checked out in a privileged workflow (.github/workflows/ci.yml)
findings.observed: .github/workflows/ci.yml runs on pull_request_target and references the pull request head at line 10.
findings.expected: Workflows triggered by pull_request_target or workflow_run do not check out or run code from the pull request.
findings.risk: These triggers run with secrets and a write token. Checking out the PR head lets anyone who opens a pull request run code with them ("pwn request").
findings.recommendation: Use the pull_request trigger for anything that builds or tests PR code. Keep pull_request_target for labelling or commenting, without checking out the head.
findings.example:
on: pull_request          # untrusted code, no secrets, read-only token
permissions:
  contents: read

findings.title: Environment file committed: .env
findings.observed: .env is tracked by git and assigns 3 variable(s). Secret-looking variables: DATABASE_URL, STRIPE_SECRET_KEY. Values are not shown.
findings.expected: Environment files with real values stay out of version control. Only templates such as .env.example are committed, and .gitignore excludes .env files.
findings.risk: A committed .env file usually holds live credentials, which are then exposed to everyone with repository access and remain in git history.
findings.recommendation: Rotate any credentials the file contains, remove it from git with `git rm --cached`, add `.env*` to .gitignore, and commit a .env.example with empty values instead.
findings.example:
# .gitignore
.env
.env.*
!.env.example

findings.title: Hard-coded Stripe live key
findings.observed: A Stripe live key (sk_l********) is present in .env at line 3. The value is redacted.
findings.expected: No secrets in source, config files, images or history. Secrets are loaded at runtime from a secrets manager or environment.
findings.risk: Anyone with read access to the repository, its forks or its history can use the credential. Leaked keys are routinely harvested within minutes of a public push.
findings.recommendation: Revoke and rotate the credential first, then remove it from the code and load it from a secrets manager or environment variable. Rewriting git history does not un-leak a pushed secret.

findings.title: Hard-coded private key
findings.observed: A private key (key material) is present in config/deploy.pem at line 1. The value is redacted.
findings.expected: No secrets in source, config files, images or history. Secrets are loaded at runtime from a secrets manager or environment.
findings.risk: Anyone with read access to the repository, its forks or its history can use the credential. Leaked keys are routinely harvested within minutes of a public push.
findings.recommendation: Revoke and rotate the credential first, then remove it from the code and load it from a secrets manager or environment variable. Rewriting git history does not un-leak a pushed secret.

findings.title: Hard-coded AWS access key ID
findings.observed: An AWS access key ID (AKIA********) is present in src/config.js at line 3. The value is redacted.
findings.expected: No secrets in source, config files, images or history. Secrets are loaded at runtime from a secrets manager or environment.
findings.risk: Anyone with read access to the repository, its forks or its history can use the credential. Leaked keys are routinely harvested within minutes of a public push.
findings.recommendation: Revoke and rotate the credential first, then remove it from the code and load it from a secrets manager or environment variable. Rewriting git history does not un-leak a pushed secret.

findings.title: Hard-coded GitHub token
findings.observed: A GitHub token (ghp_********) is present in src/config.js at line 7. The value is redacted.
findings.expected: No secrets in source, config files, images or history. Secrets are loaded at runtime from a secrets manager or environment.
findings.risk: Anyone with read access to the repository, its forks or its history can use the credential. Leaked keys are routinely harvested within minutes of a public push.
findings.recommendation: Revoke and rotate the credential first, then remove it from the code and load it from a secrets manager or environment variable. Rewriting git history does not un-leak a pushed secret.

findings.title: JWTs accepted with the "none" algorithm
findings.observed: JWTs accepted with the "none" algorithm in src/server.js at line 31.
findings.expected: JWTs are signed with strong algorithms and validated (alg, exp, aud, iss) on every request.
findings.risk: An unverified or "none"-algorithm token lets anyone forge a session for any user.
findings.recommendation: Always verify tokens with an explicit algorithm allow-list, and check exp, aud and iss. Use decode only for logging-free inspection of already-verified tokens.

findings.title: Publicly accessible database: aws_db_instance.main
findings.observed: aws_db_instance.main sets publicly_accessible = true (detected by threesock's lightweight Terraform scanner).
findings.expected: Data stores sit in private networks, are not publicly reachable, and require authentication.
findings.risk: A publicly reachable database is one leaked or weak password away from a full data breach, and is scanned for continuously.
findings.recommendation: Turn off public accessibility, place the database in private subnets, and reach it through the application, a bastion or a private endpoint.

findings.title: Public bucket ACL on aws_s3_bucket.exports
findings.observed: aws_s3_bucket.exports sets acl = "public-read" (detected by threesock's lightweight Terraform scanner).
findings.expected: Object storage is private by default, with public access blocks enabled; public content is served through a CDN with origin access control.
findings.risk: Public buckets are one of the most common causes of large data exposures and are discovered by automated scanners.
findings.recommendation: Remove public ACLs and allUsers bindings, enable the public access block, and serve intentionally public assets through a CDN with origin access control.
findings.example:
resource "aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block" "uploads" {
  bucket                  = aws_s3_bucket.uploads.id
  block_public_acls       = true
  block_public_policy     = true
  ignore_public_acls      = true
  restrict_public_buckets = true
}

findings.title: Long-lived cloud credentials in .github/workflows/ci.yml
findings.observed: .github/workflows/ci.yml passes stored cloud keys to the workflow (line 21) instead of using OIDC.
findings.expected: Workflows assume cloud roles through OIDC federation (id-token: write), so no long-lived cloud keys are stored as CI secrets.
findings.risk: Long-lived cloud keys in CI leak through logs, forks and compromised actions, and stay valid until someone remembers to rotate them.
findings.recommendation: Configure an OIDC trust between GitHub and your cloud, assume a scoped role in the workflow, and delete the stored keys.
findings.example:
permissions:
  id-token: write
  contents: read
steps:
  - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@<sha>  # pin to a commit SHA
    with:
      role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/deploy
      aws-region: us-east-1

findings.title: Script injection risk in .github/workflows/ci.yml
findings.observed: A run step in .github/workflows/ci.yml interpolates attacker-controllable event data at line 12.
findings.expected: run: steps pass attacker-controllable values (issue titles, PR bodies, branch names) through environment variables, never `${{ }}` interpolation.
findings.risk: A crafted issue title or branch name becomes shell code running in your workflow, with its token and secrets.
findings.recommendation: Move the value into an environment variable and reference it as a quoted shell variable.

findings.title: Secret printed in .github/workflows/ci.yml
findings.observed: A run step prints a secret in .github/workflows/ci.yml at line 14.
findings.expected: Workflows never print secrets; they pass them to tools through environment variables or files.
findings.risk: Masking is best-effort: transformed or partial values slip through, and logs are readable by everyone with repository read access.
findings.recommendation: Remove the echo. Pass the secret through env and let the tool read it, or write it to a file with restricted permissions.

findings.title: write-all token permissions in .github/workflows/ci.yml
findings.observed: .github/workflows/ci.yml grants permissions: write-all at line 3.
findings.expected: Each workflow declares `permissions:` (read-only by default) and grants write scopes only to the jobs that need them. Nothing uses write-all.
findings.risk: A broad GITHUB_TOKEN lets any compromised step push code, create releases or change repository settings.
findings.recommendation: Set a read-only default at the top of each workflow and grant specific write scopes per job.
findings.example:
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  release:
    permissions:
      contents: write
      id-token: write

findings.title: Hard-coded database URL with password
findings.observed: A database URL with password (Vq8********) is present in .env at line 2. The value is redacted.
findings.expected: No secrets in source, config files, images or history. Secrets are loaded at runtime from a secrets manager or environment.
findings.risk: Anyone with read access to the repository, its forks or its history can use the credential. Leaked keys are routinely harvested within minutes of a public push.
findings.recommendation: Revoke and rotate the credential first, then remove it from the code and load it from a secrets manager or environment variable. Rewriting git history does not un-leak a pushed secret.

findings.title: IAM policy allows every action ("*")
findings.observed: IAM policy allows every action ("*") in infra/main.tf at line 25.
findings.expected: IAM roles and policies grant specific actions on specific resources; no "*" actions and no primitive owner/editor roles.
findings.risk: A wildcard policy turns any compromise of that identity into full control of the account.
findings.recommendation: Replace wildcards with the specific actions the workload needs. IAM Access Analyzer or CloudTrail-based policy generation can produce a least-privilege policy from real usage.

findings.title: Password hashed with a fast, general-purpose hash function
findings.observed: Password hashed with a fast, general-purpose hash function in src/server.js at line 27.
findings.expected: Passwords are hashed with Argon2id, bcrypt or scrypt (rubric 1.4). Fast hashes such as MD5, SHA-1 or SHA-256 are never used for passwords.
findings.risk: Fast hashes can be brute-forced at billions of guesses per second, so a database leak becomes a credential leak.
findings.recommendation: Hash passwords with Argon2id (preferred), bcrypt or scrypt through a maintained library, and rehash on next login when migrating.

findings.title: CORS allows any origin with credentials
findings.observed: src/server.js allows any (or reflected) origin at line 12 and also enables credentials.
findings.expected: Credentialed CORS is limited to an explicit allow-list of origins; wildcard or reflected origins are only used for public, credential-less APIs.
findings.risk: Any website a user visits can make authenticated requests to the API and read the responses.
findings.recommendation: Replace the wildcard or reflected origin with an explicit list of trusted origins, or drop credentials for truly public endpoints.
findings.example: app.use(cors({ origin: ['https://app.example.com'], credentials: true }));

findings.title: Dynamic evaluation of a string as code
findings.observed: Dynamic evaluation of a string as code in src/server.js at line 22.
findings.expected: Code never evaluates strings as code, never builds shell commands from strings, and never deserializes untrusted data with unsafe loaders.
findings.risk: If any part of the evaluated string or command can be influenced by a user, the result is remote code execution.
findings.recommendation: Replace dynamic evaluation with explicit logic, pass command arguments as an array without a shell, and use safe loaders (json, yaml.safe_load).

findings.title: Shell command built with string interpolation
findings.observed: Shell command built with string interpolation in src/server.js at line 23.
findings.expected: Code never evaluates strings as code, never builds shell commands from strings, and never deserializes untrusted data with unsafe loaders.
findings.risk: If any part of the evaluated string or command can be influenced by a user, the result is remote code execution.
findings.recommendation: Replace dynamic evaluation with explicit logic, pass command arguments as an array without a shell, and use safe loaders (json, yaml.safe_load).

findings.title: SSH (22) open to the internet in aws_security_group.bastion
findings.observed: aws_security_group.bastion allows ingress from 0.0.0.0/0 to SSH (22) (detected by threesock's lightweight Terraform scanner).
findings.expected: Firewall rules never allow 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0 to admin ports (SSH, RDP) or data ports (PostgreSQL, MySQL, Redis, MongoDB, ...).
findings.risk: Internet-exposed admin and database ports are scanned constantly and are a leading entry point for breaches and ransomware.
findings.recommendation: Restrict ingress to known CIDRs or security groups, and reach admin interfaces through a VPN, bastion, SSM Session Manager or an identity-aware proxy.

findings.title: SQL built from strings
findings.observed: SQL query built with template literal interpolation in src/server.js at line 24.
findings.expected: Queries use bound parameters or a query builder; user input is never concatenated or interpolated into SQL.
findings.risk: String-built SQL is the classic injection flaw: one unescaped value can read, change or delete the whole database.
findings.recommendation: Pass values as bound parameters (placeholders) or use a tagged template or query builder that parameterizes for you.

findings.title: Node TLS client with certificate rejection turned off
findings.observed: Node TLS client with certificate rejection turned off in src/server.js at line 36.
findings.expected: Every TLS client validates certificates and hostnames. Private CAs are trusted explicitly instead of turning validation off.
findings.risk: With validation off, anyone on the network path can impersonate the server and read or alter traffic, including credentials.
findings.recommendation: Remove the override. For internal or self-signed services, trust the specific CA bundle instead.

findings.title: Weak cipher (DES, 3DES, RC4, Blowfish or ECB mode)
findings.observed: Weak cipher (DES, 3DES, RC4, Blowfish or ECB mode) in src/server.js at line 41.
findings.expected: TLS endpoints and clients require at least the configured minimum version (default 1.2), and code uses modern ciphers (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305).
findings.risk: Legacy protocols and ciphers have practical attacks that expose traffic or encrypted data.
findings.recommendation: Raise the minimum TLS version to 1.2 or 1.3 and replace legacy ciphers with an authenticated cipher such as AES-256-GCM.
findings.example:
tls.createServer({ minVersion: 'TLSv1.3', key, cert });
const cipher = crypto.createCipheriv('aes-256-gcm', key, iv);

findings.title: Remote script piped straight into a shell
findings.observed: Remote script piped straight into a shell in Dockerfile at line 5.
findings.expected: Downloaded tools and scripts are verified with a checksum or signature before they run.
findings.risk: Piping a remote script to a shell runs whatever the server (or anyone who compromises it) sends, inside your build.
findings.recommendation: Download to a file, verify its checksum or signature, then run it, or install from a package manager.
findings.example:
curl -fsSLo install.sh https://example.com/install.sh
echo "<sha256>  install.sh" | sha256sum -c -
sh install.sh

findings.title: No lockfile for package.json
findings.observed: package.json declares npm dependencies but no lockfile (package-lock.json, npm-shrinkwrap.json, pnpm-lock.yaml, yarn.lock, bun.lock, bun.lockb) is committed.
findings.expected: Every dependency manifest has a committed lockfile (or hash-pinned requirements) so installs are reproducible.
findings.risk: Without a lockfile, each install can pull different, possibly compromised, versions, and a build cannot be reproduced.
findings.recommendation: Generate the lockfile with your package manager, commit it, and install with the frozen/ci mode in CI.
findings.example:
pnpm install && git add pnpm-lock.yaml       # Node
uv lock && git add uv.lock                    # Python
pip-compile --generate-hashes requirements.in # pip

findings.title: Tests do not run on pull requests
findings.observed: No workflow is triggered by pull_request.
findings.expected: A CI pipeline runs automated tests and lint on every pull request, and branch protection requires it to pass before merge.
findings.risk: Without a test gate, broken or unreviewed behaviour reaches the default branch and production.
findings.recommendation: Add a pull-request workflow that runs tests and lint, then make it a required status check.
findings.example:
on: pull_request
permissions: { contents: read }
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@<sha>
      - run: npm ci && npm run lint && npm test

findings.title: Terraform uses local state
findings.observed: No backend or cloud block was found in 1 Terraform file(s) (detected by threesock's lightweight Terraform scanner), so state is local to whoever runs apply.
findings.expected: Terraform state lives in a remote, locked, access-controlled backend, and state files are never committed.
findings.risk: State files contain secrets in plain text, and unlocked or local state lets concurrent applies corrupt infrastructure.
findings.recommendation: Configure a remote backend with locking, remove committed state from git (and rotate any secrets it held), and gitignore *.tfstate.

findings.title: No CODEOWNERS file
findings.observed: No CODEOWNERS file found in .github/, the root or docs/.
findings.expected: A CODEOWNERS file assigns an owner to every directory, with named teams on security-sensitive paths.
findings.risk: Changes to unowned code can merge without review from anyone accountable for it.
findings.recommendation: Add .github/CODEOWNERS with a catch-all owner and named teams for sensitive paths, then require code owner review in branch protection.
findings.example:
# .github/CODEOWNERS
*                 @your-org/engineering
/src/auth/        @your-org/security
/infra/           @your-org/platform

findings.title: No vulnerability disclosure policy
findings.observed: No SECURITY.md or security.txt found (looked in SECURITY.md, .github/SECURITY.md, docs/SECURITY.md, .well-known/security.txt, public/.well-known/security.txt, static/.well-known/security.txt).
findings.expected: A SECURITY.md (or /.well-known/security.txt) tells external researchers how to report a vulnerability and what response to expect.
findings.risk: Without a published channel, vulnerabilities get reported publicly, to the wrong person, or not at all.
findings.recommendation: Add SECURITY.md at the repository root with a private reporting channel, supported versions and expected response time.
findings.example:
# Security policy

## Reporting a vulnerability
Email security@example.com or use GitHub private vulnerability reporting.
We acknowledge reports within 2 business days and aim to fix Critical issues within 7 days.

findings.title: 3 actions not pinned to a SHA in .github/workflows/ci.yml
findings.observed: Unpinned: actions/checkout@v4 (line 8), some-org/setup-deploy@main (line 18), aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4 (line 19).
findings.expected: Every third-party action is pinned to a full 40-character commit SHA (with the version in a comment), so a moved tag cannot change what runs.
findings.risk: Tags can be moved. A compromised action tag (as in the tj-actions/changed-files incident) runs attacker code with your workflow's secrets.
findings.recommendation: Pin each action to the commit SHA of the release you reviewed, keep the version as a comment, and let Dependabot update the pins.
findings.example: - uses: actions/checkout@11bd71901bbe5b1630ceea73d27597364c9af683 # v4.2.2

findings.title: Deploy job without an environment: deploy
findings.observed: Job deploy in .github/workflows/ci.yml deploys or publishes without an environment, so no reviewer or branch gate applies.
findings.expected: Jobs that deploy or publish run in a GitHub environment, so required reviewers, branch restrictions and environment-scoped secrets apply.
findings.risk: Without an environment gate, anyone who can push to a triggering branch can deploy to production.
findings.recommendation: Add `environment: production` to deploy jobs and configure required reviewers and deployment branch rules on that environment.
findings.example:
jobs:
  deploy:
    environment: production
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

findings.title: Session cookie is readable from JavaScript (HttpOnly disabled)
findings.observed: Session cookie is readable from JavaScript (HttpOnly disabled) in src/server.js at line 16.
findings.expected: Session and auth cookies set HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite.
findings.risk: Without HttpOnly an XSS bug can steal sessions; without Secure the cookie can leak over plain HTTP.
findings.recommendation: Set httpOnly, secure and sameSite on every session or auth cookie. Use an environment check only to relax Secure for local HTTP development.

findings.title: JWT decoded without verifying its signature
findings.observed: JWT decoded without verifying its signature in src/server.js at line 32.
findings.expected: JWTs are signed with strong algorithms and validated (alg, exp, aud, iss) on every request.
findings.risk: An unverified or "none"-algorithm token lets anyone forge a session for any user.
findings.recommendation: Always verify tokens with an explicit algorithm allow-list, and check exp, aud and iss. Use decode only for logging-free inspection of already-verified tokens.

findings.title: No automated secret scanning
findings.observed: No Gitleaks, TruffleHog, detect-secrets or similar scanner is configured in CI, pre-commit or the repository. Platform-level push protection is checked with --github.
findings.expected: A secret scanner runs on every push or pull request (and ideally as a pre-commit hook), with push protection enabled on the hosting platform.
findings.risk: Without automated scanning, a committed credential is found by an attacker before it is found by you.
findings.recommendation: Add Gitleaks (or TruffleHog) to CI and to pre-commit, and enable GitHub secret scanning with push protection.
findings.example:
# .github/workflows/secrets.yml
on: [push, pull_request]
permissions: { contents: read }
jobs:
  gitleaks:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@<sha>  # pin to a commit SHA
        with: { fetch-depth: 0 }
      - uses: gitleaks/gitleaks-action@<sha>

findings.title: No HTTP security headers configured
findings.observed: HTTP server or web framework detected in package.json, but no security-headers middleware or CSP/HSTS configuration was found in code or config. They may be set at a CDN; if so, add an exception that says where.
findings.expected: Responses set CSP, HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options and frame protections, in code or at the edge (CDN, proxy, platform config).
findings.risk: Missing headers remove browser-side defences against XSS, clickjacking and protocol downgrade.
findings.recommendation: Add a security-headers middleware (helmet, Talisman, SecurityMiddleware) or set the headers in your proxy or platform configuration.
findings.example:
import helmet from 'helmet';
app.use(helmet({ hsts: { maxAge: 31536000, includeSubDomains: true } }));

findings.title: DOM innerHTML/outerHTML assigned without visible sanitization
findings.observed: DOM innerHTML/outerHTML assigned without visible sanitization in src/public/app.js at line 2.
findings.expected: HTML output is escaped by the framework; raw-HTML sinks are avoided or fed only sanitized content.
findings.risk: Rendering raw HTML that contains user input enables cross-site scripting: session theft and actions on the victim's behalf.
findings.recommendation: Render text through the framework's escaping. Where raw HTML is unavoidable, sanitize it with DOMPurify (or bleach) on the same line so the intent is visible.
findings.example: <div dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: DOMPurify.sanitize(html) }} />

findings.title: Plain HTTP URL to api.partner-service.com
findings.observed: http://api.partner-service.com is used in src/server.js at line 37.
findings.expected: Every external and internal service URL uses https://. Plain HTTP is limited to localhost and documentation examples.
findings.risk: Requests over plain HTTP can be read and modified in transit, including tokens and personal data.
findings.recommendation: Switch the URL to https:// and make sure the target service redirects HTTP to HTTPS with HSTS.
findings.example: const API_URL = process.env.API_URL ?? 'https://api.example.com';

findings.title: Unpinned base image node:latest
findings.observed: node:latest in Dockerfile at line 1 has no version tag or uses :latest.
findings.expected: Base images use an explicit version tag, ideally pinned by digest, from a trusted registry.
findings.risk: An untagged or :latest base image changes underneath you, so builds are not reproducible and a compromised upstream image flows straight in.
findings.recommendation: Pin base images to a version and digest, and let Dependabot or Renovate propose updates.
findings.example: FROM node:22.11.0-bookworm-slim@sha256:<digest>

findings.title: Container images are not scanned
findings.observed: The repository builds container images but no image scanner (Trivy, Grype, Snyk, Docker Scout) runs in CI.
findings.expected: Images built from this repository are scanned (Trivy, Grype, Snyk, Docker Scout) before they are pushed or deployed.
findings.risk: Base images and OS packages carry their own vulnerabilities that dependency scanning of your code does not see.
findings.recommendation: Scan each built image in CI and fail on Critical/High vulnerabilities with a fix available.
findings.example:
- uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@<sha>  # pin to a commit SHA
  with: { image-ref: 'app:${{ github.sha }}', severity: 'CRITICAL,HIGH', exit-code: '1', ignore-unfixed: true }

findings.title: Missing automated dependency updates (Dependabot or Renovate) and a dependency vulnerability scan in CI
findings.observed: No automated dependency updates (Dependabot or Renovate) and a dependency vulnerability scan in CI is configured.
findings.expected: Dependabot or Renovate keeps dependencies current, and a vulnerability scan (dependency review, OSV-Scanner, npm audit, pip-audit, govulncheck) runs in CI.
findings.risk: Known-vulnerable dependencies are the most common way attackers get in, and they are only fixed if someone notices.
findings.recommendation: Enable Dependabot (or Renovate) and add a dependency scan to pull-request CI.
findings.example:
# .github/dependabot.yml
version: 2
updates:
  - package-ecosystem: npm
    directory: /
    schedule: { interval: weekly }
  - package-ecosystem: github-actions
    directory: /
    schedule: { interval: weekly }

findings.title: `npm install` used in a build
findings.observed: Dockerfile runs npm install at line 4; use npm ci to install from the lockfile.
findings.expected: Builds install exactly what the lockfile says (npm ci, pnpm install --frozen-lockfile, pip --require-hashes).
findings.risk: `npm install` in CI can rewrite the lockfile and pull versions nobody reviewed.
findings.recommendation: Use the lockfile-respecting install command in CI and Dockerfiles.
findings.example:
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
# or
RUN pnpm install --frozen-lockfile --prod

findings.title: Sensitive paths have no code owners
findings.observed: 3 sensitive files exist but there is no CODEOWNERS file.
findings.expected: Security-sensitive paths (auth, IAM, crypto, payments, infrastructure, workflows, migrations, lockfiles) have a specific CODEOWNERS entry, not just the catch-all.
findings.risk: Changes to the riskiest code can be approved by any reviewer instead of the people accountable for it.
findings.recommendation: Add explicit CODEOWNERS entries for sensitive paths and require code owner review. Adjust what counts as sensitive with sensitivePaths in threesock.yaml.
findings.example:
/src/auth/            @your-org/security
/infra/               @your-org/platform
/.github/workflows/   @your-org/platform

findings.title: Migration without a down step
findings.observed: migrations/001_init.up.sql has no matching 001_init.down.sql.
findings.expected: Each migration has a down/downgrade step, or the repository documents how schema changes are rolled back.
findings.risk: A bad migration without a way back turns a deploy rollback into a data-recovery incident.
findings.recommendation: Write a down migration for each change, or document the expand/contract and restore procedure used instead.
findings.example:
-- 20261022_add_status.down.sql
ALTER TABLE orders DROP COLUMN status;

findings.title: .gitignore does not exclude .env files
findings.observed: .gitignore has no entry matching .env files.
findings.expected: Environment files with real values stay out of version control. Only templates such as .env.example are committed, and .gitignore excludes .env files.
findings.risk: A committed .env file usually holds live credentials, which are then exposed to everyone with repository access and remain in git history.
findings.recommendation: Rotate any credentials the file contains, remove it from git with `git rm --cached`, add `.env*` to .gitignore, and commit a .env.example with empty values instead.
findings.example:
# .gitignore
.env
.env.*
!.env.example

findings.title: Possible literal credential: smtpPassword
findings.observed: `smtpPassword` is assigned a literal value (Hun********) in src/server.js at line 20. The value is redacted.
findings.expected: Credential-like settings read their values from the environment or a secrets manager, never from string literals.
findings.risk: A literal credential in code is shared with everyone who can read the repository and is hard to rotate. This check is heuristic, so confirm each match.
findings.recommendation: Replace the literal with a value loaded at runtime. If it is not a credential, add an exception with a justification.
findings.example:
// After
const client = new Client({ password: process.env.SMTP_PASSWORD });

findings.title: No documented emergency change process
findings.observed: No document describes an emergency, hotfix or break-glass change process.
findings.expected: An emergency (hotfix / break-glass) change process is documented, including who may use it and the retroactive review it requires.
findings.risk: Without a defined path, urgent fixes bypass review informally and leave no audit trail, which auditors treat as a control failure.
findings.recommendation: Document the emergency change path: who can invoke it, what is skipped, and the retroactive review required within a set time.
findings.example:
## Emergency changes
Use only for active incidents. An on-call engineer may merge with one approval from the incident commander.
A retroactive review PR is opened within 2 business days and linked from the incident ticket.

findings.title: No documented rollback procedure
findings.observed: No runbook or document describing how to roll back a deployment was found.
findings.expected: A runbook explains how to roll back a bad release, who can do it, and how to verify it worked.
findings.risk: Under incident pressure, an undocumented rollback is slow, inconsistent and easy to get wrong.
findings.recommendation: Add a rollback section to your deployment runbook (docs/runbooks/rollback.md) and rehearse it.
findings.example:
## Rolling back a release
1. Find the last good deployment in the Deployments tab.
2. Promote it: `vercel promote <deployment-url>` (or re-run the deploy workflow for the previous tag).
3. Confirm health checks and error rates recover; post in #incidents.
